1.1 Overview
Dataset: Moser & Voena (2012) — moser_voena_didtextbook.dta
The Trading with the Enemy Act (TWEA) allowed US firms to use German-owned patents. Treatment (\(D_{g,t}\)) equals 1 for the 336 subclasses that received German patents, starting in 1919. The dataset contains 289,920 observations (7,248 subclasses × 40 years).

1.2 Green Question 1: Static TWFE Regression

Using the moser_voena_didtextbook dataset, run the TWFE regression of the number of patents in subclass \(g\) and year \(t\) on subclass and year FEs and the twea treatment, clustering standard errors at the subclass level.


StataRPython


reghdfe patents twea, absorb(subclass year) cluster(subclass)
HDFE Linear regression                            Number of obs   =    289,920
Absorbing 2 HDFE groups                           F(   1,   7247) =      54.95
                                                  R-squared       =     0.4788
Number of clusters (subclass) =      7,248        Root MSE        =     0.9904

             |               Robust
     patents | Coefficient  std. err.      t    P>|t|     [95% conf. interval]
-------------+----------------------------------------------------------------

       _cons |   .4634348   .0009464   489.67   0.000     .4615796    .4652901
------------------------------------------------------------------------------


library(fixest)
library(haven)

df <- read_dta("data/moser_voena_didtextbook.dta")
model1 <- feols(patents ~ twea | subclass + year,
                data = df, cluster = ~subclass)
summary(model1)

Observations: 289,920

---

import pandas as pd
import pyfixest as pf

df = pd.read_stata("data/moser_voena_didtextbook.dta")
m1 = pf.feols("patents ~ twea | subclass + year",
              data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "subclass"})
print(m1.summary())

1.5 Green Question 4: Event-Study TWFE Regression

Estimate the event-study TWFE regression. Test whether pre-trend coefficients are jointly significant. Verify that \(\hat{\beta}_1^{fe}\) equals the DID from equation (3.7).


StataRPython


reg patents i.year treatmentgroup reltimeminus* reltimeplus*, cluster(subclass)

* F-test on pre-trends
test reltimeminus1 reltimeminus2 ... reltimeminus18
       F( 18,  7247) =    3.79
            Prob > F =    0.0000
* Verify equation (3.7) for l=1
quietly summarize patents if year==1919 & treatmentgroup==1
scalar m1 = r(mean)
quietly summarize patents if year==1918 & treatmentgroup==1
scalar m2 = r(mean)
quietly summarize patents if year==1919 & treatmentgroup==0
scalar m3 = r(mean)
quietly summarize patents if year==1918 & treatmentgroup==0
scalar m4 = r(mean)
display "DID manual = " m1-m2-(m3-m4)
DID manual (eq 3.7, l=1) = .02352017


event_formula <- as.formula(paste(
  "patents ~ i(year) + treatmentgroup +",
  paste(paste0("reltimeminus", 1:18), collapse = " + "), "+",
  paste(paste0("reltimeplus", 1:21), collapse = " + ")))
model4 <- feols(event_formula, data = df, cluster = ~subclass)

# F-test on pre-trends
library(car)
linearHypothesis(model4, paste0("reltimeminus", 1:18))

# DID manual
m1 <- mean(df$patents[df$year == 1919 & df$treatmentgroup == 1])
m2 <- mean(df$patents[df$year == 1918 & df$treatmentgroup == 1])
m3 <- mean(df$patents[df$year == 1919 & df$treatmentgroup == 0])
m4 <- mean(df$patents[df$year == 1918 & df$treatmentgroup == 0])
cat("DID manual:", m1 - m2 - (m3 - m4))
Chisq = 68.25, p-value = 8.915e-08

DID manual (eq 3.7, l=1): 0.02352017
reltimeplus1 coef:         0.02352017


import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

minus_vars = [f"reltimeminus{i}" for i in range(1, 19)]
plus_vars  = [f"reltimeplus{i}"  for i in range(1, 22)]
all_reltime = minus_vars + plus_vars

fml_es = "patents ~ " + " + ".join(all_reltime) + " + treatmentgroup | year"
m4 = pf.feols(fml_es, data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "subclass"})

# F-test on pre-trends
c = m4.coef()
v_mat = pd.DataFrame(m4._vcov, index=c.index, columns=c.index)
pre_names = [x for x in minus_vars if x in c.index]
beta_pre = c[pre_names].values
V_pre = v_mat.loc[pre_names, pre_names].values
F_stat = beta_pre @ np.linalg.inv(V_pre) @ beta_pre / len(pre_names)
p_val = 1 - stats.f.cdf(F_stat, len(pre_names), df["subclass"].nunique() - 1)
print(f"F-test: F({len(pre_names)}, {df['subclass'].nunique()-1}) = {F_stat:.4f}, p = {p_val:.4f}")

# DID manual
m1v = df.loc[(df["year"]==1919) & (df["treatmentgroup"]==1), "patents"].mean()
m2v = df.loc[(df["year"]==1918) & (df["treatmentgroup"]==1), "patents"].mean()
m3v = df.loc[(df["year"]==1919) & (df["treatmentgroup"]==0), "patents"].mean()
m4v = df.loc[(df["year"]==1918) & (df["treatmentgroup"]==0), "patents"].mean()
print(f"DID manual (eq 3.7, l=1): {m1v - m2v - (m3v - m4v):.8f}")
print(f"reltimeplus1 coef:        {m4.coef()['reltimeplus1']:.8f}")
F-test: F(18, 7247) = 3.7917, p = 0.0000

DID manual (eq 3.7, l=1): 0.02352017
reltimeplus1 coef:        0.02352017



Result: Pre-trends are jointly significant (\(F = 3.79\), \(p < 0.001\)). The manual DID (0.02352) matches reltimeplus1 exactly.

1.7 Green Question 6: Linear Pre-Trends We Could Fail to Detect

Use the pretrends package (Roth, 2022) to compute the slope detectable with 50% power using 6 pre-periods.


StataRPython


reghdfe patents reltimeminus* reltimeplus*, absorb(treatmentgroup year) cluster(subclass)
pretrends power 0.5, numpre(6)
Slope for 50% power =  .0098235


library(pretrends)
# Extract coefficients and vcov for first 6 pre-periods
pretrend_coefs_6 <- paste0("reltimeminus", 1:6)
beta <- coef(model6)[pretrend_coefs_6]
sigma <- vcov(model6)[pretrend_coefs_6, pretrend_coefs_6]
slope50 <- slope_for_power(sigma = sigma, targetPower = 0.5,
                           tVec = -6:-1, referencePeriod = 0)
cat("Slope for 50% power:", slope50)
Slope for 50% power (numpre=6): 0.009796021


from scipy import optimize

short_minus = [f"reltimeminus{i}" for i in range(1, 7)]
fml_pre = "patents ~ " + " + ".join(short_minus + plus_vars) + " | treatmentgroup + year"
m6 = pf.feols(fml_pre, data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "subclass"})
coefs_pre = m6.coef()
vcov_pre = pd.DataFrame(m6._vcov, index=coefs_pre.index, columns=coefs_pre.index)
pre6 = [v for v in short_minus if v in coefs_pre.index]
V_pre6 = vcov_pre.loc[pre6, pre6].values
n_pre = len(pre6); dfd = df["subclass"].nunique() - 1

def power_at_slope(slope):
    mu = np.array([slope * (-int(v.replace("reltimeminus", ""))) for v in pre6])
    ncp = mu @ np.linalg.inv(V_pre6) @ mu
    cv = stats.f.ppf(0.95, n_pre, dfd)
    return 1 - stats.ncf.cdf(cv, n_pre, dfd, ncp)

slope_50 = optimize.brentq(lambda s: power_at_slope(s) - 0.5, 0.0001, 1.0)
print(f"Slope for 50% power (numpre=6): {slope_50:.6f}")
Slope for 50% power (numpre=6): 0.008878



Note: Stata and R use the official pretrends package (Roth 2022) and give ≈0.0098. Python uses a manual F-test-based implementation and gives ≈0.0089. The difference is due to the underlying distributional assumptions (multivariate normal vs. non-central F).

1.8 Green Question 7: Variance of Treatment Effects

Compare the variance of diffpatentswrt1918 in treatment and control groups in 1932.


StataRPython


sdtest diffpatentswrt1918 if year==1932, by(treatmentgroup)

scalar sd_effects = r(sd_2) - r(sd_1)
reg diffpatentswrt1918 treatmentgroup if year==1932
display "CI: [" _b[treatmentgroup] - 1.96*sd_effects ", " _b[treatmentgroup] + 1.96*sd_effects "]"
Variance ratio test
--------------------------------------------------------------
   Group |     Obs      Std. dev.
---------+------------------------
       0 |   6,912      1.772807
       1 |     336      2.011905
--------------------------------------------------------------
    ratio = sd(0) / sd(1)                        f =   0.7764
  Pr(F < f) = 0.0004     2*Pr(F < f) = 0.0008

sd_2 - sd_1 = .23909779
beta = .64221644
CI: [.17358476, 1.1108481]


df_1932 <- df %>% filter(year == 1932)
var_test <- var.test(diffpatentswrt1918 ~ treatmentgroup, data = df_1932)
print(var_test)

sd_stats <- df_1932 %>% group_by(treatmentgroup) %>%
  summarise(sd = sd(diffpatentswrt1918, na.rm = TRUE))
sd_effects <- sd_stats$sd[2] - sd_stats$sd[1]
effect_reg <- lm(diffpatentswrt1918 ~ treatmentgroup, data = df_1932)
beta_reg <- coef(effect_reg)["treatmentgroup"]
cat("CI: [", beta_reg - 1.96*sd_effects, ",", beta_reg + 1.96*sd_effects, "]")
F = 0.77644, p-value = 0.0008145
SD control: 1.772807
SD treated: 2.011905
sd_2 - sd_1 = 0.2390978
beta = 0.6422164
CI: [ 0.1735848 , 1.110848 ]


df_1932 = df[df["year"] == 1932]
g0 = df_1932.loc[df_1932["treatmentgroup"] == 0, "diffpatentswrt1918"].dropna()
g1 = df_1932.loc[df_1932["treatmentgroup"] == 1, "diffpatentswrt1918"].dropna()
sd0, sd1 = g0.std(ddof=1), g1.std(ddof=1)
sd_effects = sd1 - sd0
F_var = sd0**2 / sd1**2
p_two = 2 * min(stats.f.cdf(F_var, len(g0)-1, len(g1)-1),
                1 - stats.f.cdf(F_var, len(g0)-1, len(g1)-1))
m7 = pf.feols("diffpatentswrt1918 ~ treatmentgroup", data=df_1932)
beta = m7.coef()["treatmentgroup"]
print(f"F = {F_var:.4f}, p = {p_two:.4f}")
print(f"sd_2 - sd_1 = {sd_effects:.6f}")
print(f"beta = {beta:.6f}")
print(f"CI: [{beta - 1.96*sd_effects:.6f}, {beta + 1.96*sd_effects:.6f}]")
SD control: 1.772923
SD treated: 2.011905
sd_2 - sd_1 = 0.238982
F = 0.7765, 2*Pr(F<f) = 0.0008
beta = 0.642216
CI: [0.173812, 1.110620]



Result: The treated group has a larger variance (\(\hat{\sigma}_1 = 2.01 > \hat{\sigma}_0 = 1.77\)). The implied SD of treatment effects is \(\approx 0.239\), and the confidence interval for \(\beta_{14}\) using this SD is \([0.174, 1.111]\).

import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

df = pd.read_stata("data/moser_voena_didtextbook.dta")

plus_vars = [f"reltimeplus{i}" for i in range(1, 22)]

fml = "patents ~ " + " + ".join(minus_vars + plus_vars) + \
      " | year_x_pat1900 + treatmentgroup"
# Create interaction variable
df["year_x_pat1900"] = df["year"].astype(str) + "_" + \
                        df["patents1900"].astype(str)
m = pf.feols(fml, data=df, vcov={"CRV1": "subclass"})
print(m.summary())

# F-test on pre-trends
c = m.coef()
v_mat = pd.DataFrame(m._vcov, index=c.index, columns=c.index)
pre_names = [x for x in minus_vars if x in c.index]
beta_pre = c[pre_names].values
V_pre = v_mat.loc[pre_names, pre_names].values
F_stat = beta_pre @ np.linalg.inv(V_pre) @ beta_pre / len(pre_names)
p_val = 1 - stats.f.cdf(F_stat, len(pre_names),
                          df["subclass"].nunique() - 1)
print(f"F-test: F({len(pre_names)}, {df['subclass'].nunique()-1})"
      f" = {F_stat:.4f}, p = {p_val:.4f}")

# Correlation test
corr = pf.feols("patents1900 ~ treatmentgroup",
    data=df[df["year"] == 1900])
print(corr.summary())

3.1 Overview
Dataset: Gentzkow, Shapiro and Sinkinson (2011) — gentzkowetal_didtextbook.dta
This chapter investigates what the TWFE estimator \(\hat{\beta}_{fe}\) estimates outside the classical design, using the effect of newspapers on voter turnout. The design features a non-binary treatment (number of newspapers), non-absorbing treatment changes, and variation in treatment timing across 1,195 US counties from 1872 to 1928.
Key tool: the twowayfeweights package (Stata/R) decomposes \(\hat{\beta}_{fe}\) into a weighted sum of treatment effects, where some weights may be negative — meaning \(\hat{\beta}_{fe}\) may not estimate a convex combination of effects.
No plots in this chapter — only numerical outputs from regressions and decompositions.

Dataset: Wolfers (2006) — wolfers2006_didtextbook.dta

5.1 Overview
Dataset: Pierce & Schott (2016) — pierce_schott_didtextbook.dta
This chapter applies the Heterogeneous Adoption Design (HAD) framework to study how China’s permanent normal trade relations (PNTR) status affected US manufacturing employment. The key feature: treatment is continuous (the NTR gap, ranging from 0.02 to 0.64), not binary. All 103 US industries are “treated” — there are no pure control groups, but industries with near-zero NTR gaps serve as quasi-stayers.
Key tools: twowayfeweights for weight decomposition, and the stute_test package for testing whether \(E[\Delta Y | D]\) is linear in \(D\) (Stute, 1997). Standard errors use HC2 heteroskedasticity-robust estimation throughout.
No figures in this chapter — only numerical outputs.

title: 6  Chapter 8: General Designs
text:
6.1 Overview
Dataset: Gentzkow, Shapiro & Sinkinson (2011) — gentzkowetal_didtextbook.dta
This chapter studies general designs where the treatment may be non-binary (taking values 0, 1, 2, …) and/or non-absorbing (groups can enter and exit treatment), and where treatment lags may affect the outcome. The running example uses the same Gentzkow et al. (2011) dataset from Chapter 5: a US county \(\times\) presidential-election panel (1,195 counties, 1872–1928), measuring the effect of the number of daily newspapers (numdailies) on voter turnout (prestout).
Key topics: static TWFE decompositions with multiple treatments (twowayfeweights), non-normalized and normalized event-study estimators (did_multiplegt_dyn), treatment-path descriptions (design option), and heterogeneity-robust estimators ruling out dynamic effects (did_multiplegt_stat).
7 Green Questions + 2 Figures + 1 Bonus test.
